result: The optorepressilator is an optically controllable genetic clock combining the repressilator with an optogenetic module (CcaS-CcaR system) that produces LacI from two genes, with the light-controlled component (x') decoupled from other repressors and determined only by light.
evaluation: All reviewers affirm the successful development of the optorepressilator system. Reviewer 1 states 'the planned system was achieved,' Reviewer 2 confirms 'the authors successfully kept the original repressilator oscillation when the added promoter was not activated,' and Reviewer 3 notes 'the study provides a simple and elegant mechanism' with 'the design relies on optogenetic proteins.'

result: Controlling promoter leakage under red light was crucial for optorepressilator function. Four expression ranges were tested by modulating transcription and translation; only the lowest expression level (weak RBS + genome insertion, ~1500-fold reduction) maintained oscillations comparable to control, while higher LacI expression destroyed the limit cycle.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly affirms this optimization: 'The authors correctly identified the main optimization goal, namely the effective leakiness of their construct even under red light. Then, they successfully overcame this issue using synthetic biology approaches.' This demonstrates reviewer recognition of both the challenge and its successful resolution.

result: Transient green light exposure synchronizes optorepressilator populations, causing CFP fluorescence to decay to zero during 12-hour green light exposure, with single-cell mother-machine data confirming most channels blink in unison after synchronizing light is removed.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 confirms 'the authors showed that it is possible to synchronise the phase of the oscillation' and Reviewer 3 notes 'exposure to green light causes overexpression of the lacI, pushing the system into a specific state. Consequently, returning to red light will restore the oscillations from the same phase in all cells, effectively synchronizing the cell population.'

result: Periodic light pulses entrain optorepressilators to oscillate indefinitely with high contrast undamped oscillations at the population level, confirmed by both plate reader and mother machine experiments, with slower-growing cells receiving pulses on rising edges and faster-growing cells on falling edges to synchronize periods.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 states 'by changing the frequency of the short pulses, the repressilator was entrained to various ratios to the pulse period,' and Reviewer 3 notes 'periodic exposure to green light enables efficient entrainment.' Reviewer 1 affirms 'the comparison with a mathematical model, population, and single-cell measurements demonstrate convincingly that the planned system was achieved.'

result: The optorepressilator displays a phase-sensitive response to light pulses similar to natural circadian clocks, where positive pulse arrival phase delays oscillations and negative phase advances them, with the exact phase response curve shape depending on light intensity and pulse duration.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 confirms 'the authors showed that it is possible to synchronise the phase of the oscillation, especially when the activation happens as a short pulse at the right phase of the repressilator oscillation.' Reviewer 3 notes the system demonstrates 'how periodic exposure to green light enables efficient entrainment' with phase-dependent effects.

result: The optorepressilator exhibits Arnold's tongues (synchronization regions) when detuned from natural frequency, with experimental validation showing all predicted synchronization regimes including 1:1, 2:1, and 1:2 frequency locking in both plate reader and mother machine experiments.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly states 'the author could reconstruct the so-called "Arnold tongues", the signature of entrainment of the nonlinear oscillator to externally added periodic perturbation.' Reviewer 3 notes the authors 'show how...the frequency of the forcing signal affects the oscillatory behavior (detuning).'

result: The entrainment mechanism is robust and quantitatively understood from single cell to population level through a simple protein-only mathematical model that provides analytical predictions for phase response curves, amplitude-period correlations, and robustness against leakage.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'the comparison with a mathematical model, population, and single-cell measurements demonstrate convincingly that the planned system was achieved.' Reviewer 2 notes 'the behaviour is consistent with the simplified mathematical model,' and Reviewer 3 affirms 'the work is supported by a simplified model of the repressilator...The model predictions are well aligned with the experimental evidence.'

result: Cell-to-cell variability in growth rates causes dispersion in oscillator periods, leading to progressive desynchronization with population oscillation amplitude reduced to half after ~2.5 periods (16-hour period observed in IPTG-synchronized cultures).
evaluation: Reviewer 2 acknowledges 'when many cells oscillate, their phases tend to desynchronize,' which is the fundamental problem the optorepressilator addresses. This desynchronization phenomenon is accepted as the motivation for the entrainment approach, with no reviewer questioning these baseline observations.

result: The period difference between optorepressilator and control strains is explained by additional plasmids causing lower growth rate, with the repressilator period mainly controlled by inverse growth rate; when time is normalized by growth rate, oscillations overlap.
evaluation: This mechanistic explanation is not questioned by any reviewer. Reviewer 3 notes the system's successful optimization without raising concerns about growth rate effects, implicitly accepting this interpretation as part of the validated model-experiment agreement.

result: The entrainment mechanism is reminiscent of natural circadian clocks, with phase response curves predicting system response to periodic inputs and stable entrained states occurring at fixed points with negative slope satisfying specific conditions.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly states the authors 'sought to make this oscillator entrainable by an external forcing signal, analogous to the way natural biological oscillators (like the circadian clock) are synchronized.' The analogy to circadian clocks is accepted as valid by reviewers discussing the phase-sensitive response.

result: The optorepressilator enriches the synthetic biology toolbox as a light-synchronizable clock with advantages over chemical signaling, including instant application/removal, spatial addressability, and potential applications in bioreactors and in vivo settings with infrared systems.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'this toolbox is valuable, contributing both to bioengineering and to the understanding of biological dynamical systems.' Reviewer 3 notes 'the study provides an important demonstration of engineering tunability into a foundational genetic circuit, expands the synthetic biology toolbox, and provides a platform to address critical questions.'

result: The model predicts that phase response curve shape depends on light intensity (β') and pulse duration (τ), with model predictions shown in appendix figures but limited experimental validation across different pulse parameters.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 raises a significant concern: 'The entire work makes use of a single intensity and single duration of the green pulse to force entrainment. While the model has clear predictions for how different modalities should affect entrainment, more experiments are needed to validate those predictions.' This indicates the theoretical predictions are accepted but experimental validation is incomplete.

result: The optorepressilator can be entrained even when forcing period deviates substantially from natural frequency, demonstrating flexibility in entrainment range.
evaluation: While Reviewer 3 notes 'even after optimizing the expression level of the light-sensitive gene, the system is very sensitive, i.e., a very short exposure is sufficient to elicit the strongest entertainment. This limited dynamic range might hamper some model testing and future usage.' This suggests the entrainment works but with limitations not fully explored.

result: The optorepressilator represents a four-node synthetic oscillatory network that locks phase to external periodic light signals through a mechanism where pulses can delay or advance the clock depending on arrival time, enabling entrainment across a range of forcing frequencies.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 raises a conceptual concern: 'the system is entrained by transiently "breaking" the oscillator: each pulse of green light represents a Hopf bifurcation into a single attractor. it means that the system cannot oscillate in constant green light. In comparison, this is generally not the case for natural zeitgebers...While the approach presented in this manuscript is valid, a comprehensive analysis of more subtle modes of repressilator entrainment could also be of value.' This suggests the mechanism works but differs fundamentally from natural systems.
